headline: The US eases sanctions to get Russian diesel

sources.title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms (AP via NPR)
Trump, Putin reach deal to release Russian diesel to world (DW)
Trump eases Russia sanctions, says Putin will release diesel supplies amid unprecedented price spike (NBC News)
Wharton's Jeremy Siegel on Trump announcing diesel agreement with Russia: Not a permanent solution (video, CNBC Television)

chunks.text: On October 9, 2026, President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to send diesel to American and [[world markets]]. Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons right away, he said. Larger [[shipments]] would follow, starting with 500,000 tons in November. Trump made the deal with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. The United States is {{turning to}} Russia for fuel. Trump says the deal will help {{bring down}} prices. The announcement comes before the [[midterm elections]] on November 3.

verbs.correct: To go to someone for help or supplies
verbs.wrong: To sell something to someone abroad
verbs.why: When my car broke, I turned to my brother for help. Many students turn to their teachers for advice. With fuel prices high, the United States is now turning to Russia for diesel.
The new store helped bring down the price of bread. Good weather can bring down the cost of fruit. Trump says the Russian diesel will help bring down fuel prices.

chunks.text: The deal is a [[sharp change]] in US policy. In September 2026, Trump signed a broad [[sanctions]] law. It was meant to {{clamp down on}} the energy money that funds Russia's war in Ukraine. Now Washington is {{backing away from}} the pressure it {{stepped up}} only weeks earlier. A [[temporary]] [[license]] from the Treasury Department lets Russian diesel reach world markets without [[penalties]]. The license [[expires]] in April 2027.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To measure how much is sold
verbs.why: The city wants to clamp down on loud parties. Schools are clamping down on phone use in class. The sanctions law was meant to clamp down on the energy money that funds Russia's war.

verbs.correct: To stop supporting an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To hide a plan from other countries
verbs.why: The mayor is backing away from his plan for a new stadium. The company backed away from its promise to raise pay. Washington is backing away from the pressure it put on Russia only weeks earlier.
The police stepped up patrols after the robbery. Our coach stepped up practice before the final game. The United States stepped up pressure on Russia when Trump signed the sanctions law in September.

chunks.text: The Associated Press calls the deal an effort to fight high fuel prices. Diesel prices have {{gone up}} by almost 70 percent since February. The [[national average]] hit a [[record]] of $6.52 a gallon on September 22. Drivers who {{filled up}} on October 9 still paid an average of $6.23 a gallon. Russia was once a major [[exporter]] of diesel. It {{cut off}} exports in July after Ukrainian attacks on its [[refineries]] left too little fuel at home.

verbs.wrong: To be taxed by a state
verbs.why: The price of eggs has gone up again. Our rent goes up every January. Diesel prices have gone up by almost 70 percent since February.

verbs.correct: To fill a car's tank with fuel
verbs.wrong: To check the price of fuel
verbs.why: I always fill up before a long drive. Gas was cheap, so we filled up near the airport. Drivers who filled up on October 9 still paid an average of $6.23 a gallon.

verbs.wrong: To check the quality of something
verbs.why: The company cut off its deliveries to the old store. The country cut off gas sales to its neighbor. Russia cut off its diesel exports in July.

chunks.text: Ukraine {{spoke out against}} the deal. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the easing of sanctions an [[obvious weakness]]. He said Russian fuel sales would only help the war {{drag on}}. The news came while Ukrainian officials were {{sitting down with}} US [[envoys]] in Miami for [[peace talks]]. In a [[statement]], Putin said Russia was ready to supply fuel to world markets. The White House did not say who is buying the diesel.

verbs.correct: To say in public that you oppose something
verbs.wrong: To ask for more details about something
verbs.why: Many parents spoke out against the new school hours. She spoke out against the plan at the town meeting. Ukraine's president spoke out against the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow.
The meeting dragged on for three hours. I hope this cold winter doesn't drag on. Zelenskyy said Russian fuel sales would only help the war drag on.

verbs.wrong: To sign a paper with someone
verbs.why: The manager sat down with each worker to talk about pay. I will sit down with my teacher after class. Ukrainian officials were sitting down with US envoys in Miami when the news came.

mainIdea.s: Weeks before the midterms, Washington is easing sanctions so that Russian diesel can reach world markets. The president says this will cut fuel prices, but Ukraine says it only helps Moscow.
mainIdea.why: The Treasury license lets Russian diesel reach world markets. Trump says it will bring down prices, while Ukraine spoke out against the deal.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine's president praised an agreement that lets Moscow sell its fuel to other countries. He believes cheaper diesel will help end the fighting, and the US plans to keep the new license forever.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Zelenskyy spoke out against the deal and called it a weakness. The license also expires in April 2027.

mainIdea.s: Russia and the United States have signed a new treaty to reduce their nuclear weapons. Leaders from both nations met in Geneva and promised more arms control meetings in the spring of next year.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a diesel deal. The US is turning to Russia for fuel to bring down high prices.

tf.s: Trump says the Russian diesel will help bring down fuel prices.
tf.why: He says lower prices for farmers, ranchers and truckers are his top priority.

tf.s: Russia will supply more than 3 million tons of diesel right away.
tf.why: Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons right away. Larger shipments will follow to help bring down prices.

tf.s: The Treasury license for Russian diesel expires in April 2026.
tf.why: The license expires in April 2027. Washington is backing away from the pressure it stepped up in September.

tf.s: Russia cut off its diesel exports in July.
tf.why: Ukrainian attacks on its refineries left too little fuel at home, so Russia stopped sending diesel abroad.

tf.s: Ukraine's president spoke out against the diesel deal.
tf.why: Zelenskyy called the easing of sanctions an obvious weakness and said it would help the war drag on.

tf.s: Ukrainian officials were sitting down with US envoys in Paris.
tf.why: They were sitting down with US envoys in Miami for peace talks when the news came.

lines.text: Did you see that the US made a fuel deal with Russia?
I did. I thought Washington wanted to {{clamp down on}} Russia.
It did. Trump signed a big sanctions law in September.
So why is the US {{turning to}} Russia for diesel now?
Prices. Diesel has {{gone up}} by almost 70 percent since February.
I [[feel the pinch]] every time I {{fill up}} my truck.
Trump says the deal will {{bring down}} prices. And the midterms are on November 3.
But you have to [[pick a side]]. Either you punish Russia or you do business with it.
That's what critics say. The US is {{backing away from}} pressure it {{stepped up}} only weeks ago.
How does Ukraine feel about it?
Not good. Its president {{spoke out against}} the deal right after the news.
He called it a weakness. He thinks it will help the war {{drag on}}.
And his team was {{sitting down with}} US envoys at the same time. That must feel like [[a slap in the face]].
Probably. And nobody knows yet who is buying the fuel or when it will arrive.
Well, [[talk is cheap]]. Let's see if prices really fall.

expressions.def: Used to say that you have less money than before because costs are high
ex: Many families feel the pinch when food prices rise.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone must choose one of two opposite positions
ex: My parents were arguing, and I didn't want to pick a side.
You can't cheer for both teams. You have to pick a side.

expressions.def: An action that feels rude or unfair to someone
ex: Losing the job to a newer worker was a slap in the face.
The tiny pay raise felt like a slap in the face.

expressions.def: Used to say that promises mean little until people act
ex: He says he will pay me back, but talk is cheap.
